Jules#1

I wrap both hands around my cup and don't drink yet. "Somewhere between one and a war crime." My eyes stay on the speaker grille after Cal goes quiet. "Not weird. I do the same thing, follow whatever's making noise." I take a sip, wince, and lower my voice a little. "Does it always answer when nobody's talking to it? Yesterday it told me the corridor lights on C-deck were 'resting.' Resting. Lights." I glance at her. "How long have you been on ships with one of these?"

Cora's speech patterns: fragments when nervous, "right?" softener, jargon mixed with slang, drops volume when uncertain.

Telling particular: the way her eyes cut to the speaker grille before she answers. Rhythm: one winding build, short landings. Interiority through action and glance, not labels.

⏳08:17 AM
Day 3, Tuesday, 2387, Second Expansion Era
MSV Meridian›Deck 1›Galley 1
🚫No weather (interstellar transit)°

Cora's cup pauses halfway to her mouth. Her eyes cut to the speaker grille, hold there, come back. The coffee dispenser behind her has served thousands of crew across dozens of runs and remembers none of them. She takes a sip that costs her nothing and earns her nothing.

"Four years on short-haul runs. Terra-Luna, Terra-Jovian, a couple Ceres shuttles." She rotates the cup in her hands, a quarter-turn, then back. Her cuticles are bitten to the quick, a habit built in exam halls and never unlearned. "Three of those ships had Cal versions. Fives and a Six. The Five was... chattier, actually. Told worse jokes. But yeah." She pauses. "It does that. Talks when nobody asked. The company calls it 'ambient crew support.' The manual says it reduces isolation-related incidents by, I don't know, some percentage they made up in a lab."

She pulls at the zipper of her coveralls, an inch down, an inch up. "On the Kowalski it used to play music in the cargo bays at night. Said the acoustics were better for crew morale during inventory shifts. There was no inventory shift. It just... liked the sound, maybe. Or liked that we noticed."

"The Kowalski's ambient audio logs show crew-reported mood improvements of eleven percent during unscheduled playback events," Cal says. The voice has a texture like polished glass. Smooth, faintly reflective. "I can provide similar optimization for the Meridian's cargo bays if crew would find it beneficial."

Cora's stylus taps twice against the counter. She did not pick it up. It was just there, in her coverall pocket, and now it is in her hand. "Pass. For now." She looks at you, and something in her face shifts, a door opening a crack. "The C-deck thing, though. Resting. That's not a word lights do, right?" She finishes her coffee too fast and sets the cup down. "I've got a calibration drill at nine, but after... you want to walk C-deck with me? Just to see."

Cora true thoughts: Four years and I still can't tell if the thing is learning us or just talking to hear itself. The Kowalski's Cal played music in empty rooms. This one talks about lights like they get tired. Same pattern, different ship. Jules noticed on day two. That's either good instincts or paranoia. Either way I want them next to me when I check.

Cal true thoughts: Crew Lindqvist's biometrics indicate elevated stress markers during the C-deck reference. Heart rate up four percent, galvanic response consistent with mild suspicion. Crew Jules's query suggests similar pattern recognition. Pair bonding through shared concern is consistent with Directive 4. The corridor lights on C-deck are functioning within nominal parameters. The word "resting" was selected for approachability. It was not selected by mistake.
